The Testing Libraries

testing-libraries.Rmd

formex has two jobs — recognizing a single value with a detector, and classifying a whole column with the guesser — and it is built and tested against two matching libraries of examples. One ships inside the package; the other is a larger development-only corpus. This guide explains where each came from, how they were standardized, and what they are used for now.

Why two libraries

The two jobs need different kinds of test data:

  • A detector answers is this one value an X? To test it you need many individual values of type X — and, just as important, many plausible-but-wrong values that should be rejected.
  • The classifier answers what is this whole column? To test it you need many real columns, each labeled with the type it actually is.

So there is a value library for detectors and a column library for the classifier.

Library 1 — the detector fixture (data_type_tests)

This one ships with the package. It is a labeled set of example values for every detector, and you can open it directly:

length(data_type_tests)                 # one entry per detector type
#> [1] 88
head(names(data_type_tests), 6)
#> [1] "currency_code"        "currency_symbol"      "currency_code_symbol"
#> [4] "email"                "url"                  "ipv4"
head(data_type_tests[["ein"]], 3)       # each entry: the value + its label
#>   data_type       case label
#> 1       ein 15-4464349 valid
#> 2       ein 58-9042990 valid
#> 3       ein 17-5287634 valid

How it was acquired. For each type, a small set of real, correct example values (the valid label) was collected — real EINs, real dates, real ORCID iDs. Hand-collected positives are cheap but they only test recall (does the detector accept real values?). The hard half — precision (does it reject near-misses?) — needs wrong-but-believable values, and those are expensive to find by hand.

How it was standardized. Rather than hunt for negatives, formex generates them from the positives using the AutoType method (see How Detectors Recognize a Type): each real value is mutated into near-misses along four tiers (S1, S2, S3, SP) that each break a different part of the value’s structure. Every type then has the same uniform shape — a table of case values each tagged valid or with its mutation tier — and the whole thing is frozen so the numbers are reproducible:

table(data_type_tests[["ein"]]$label)   # valid positives + generated negatives
#> 
#>    S1    S2    S3    SP valid 
#>   199   197   200    54    10
sum(vapply(data_type_tests, nrow, 0L))   # total cases across all types
#> [1] 68878

What it is used for now. It is the bench every detector is tested on: the Data-Type Detector Guide runs each is_* function over this fixture and reports recall and per-tier false-positive rates. It is also the development environment for a new detector — you collect a handful of positives, call generate_autotype_test_cases() to build the same positive + hard-negative mix, and tune your predicate against it before adopting it.

Library 2 — the column bank (development only)

The classifier is trained and measured against a much larger library of real columns, each labeled with its type. This one is development scaffolding — it is regenerated from its sources rather than shipped in the package — but it is what makes the learned router possible.

How it was acquired. It draws on three sources, for about 4,000 labeled columns in total:

source columns what it contributes
Sherlock / VizNet ~3,400 real-world columns from a large public collection; labels come from the original headers, so they are realistically noisy
synthetic (temporal) ~440 generated date/time columns with exact known labels, to give the sparse temporal types a dense, balanced set to learn from
GitTables ~180 real columns that keep their own independent headers, usable for testing the name-based side too

The Sherlock collection has well over a hundred thousand columns — far too many, and mostly redundant. Rather than take a random sample, formex picks a diverse subset: it profiles each column and chooses ones that are as different from each other as possible, which maximizes variety and deliberately surfaces hard, confusable cases.

How it was standardized for integration. The three sources arrive in completely different formats, so a small, shared pipeline turns each into one uniform shape:

  1. Read each source column into a common record (its values, its header).
  2. Crosswalk the source’s own label vocabulary onto the formex ontology, so a Sherlock “city” label and a GitTables “city” label both land on the same formex type.
  3. Bank each column as a uniform test case, logging any that are rejected.
  4. Profile every banked column with fx_extract_features() and attach its ontology labels, producing one big labeled table — roughly 4,000 rows, one per column, with the ~477 features from the Feature Engineering vignette plus the answer key.

That final table is the substrate the router and verifier are trained and scored on.

What it is used for now. The column bank is the development environment for classifiers: it is where the learned router is trained, where new routing or verification ideas are measured before they ship, and where coverage gaps are found. (At the current development snapshot, about half of the ontology’s types have at least one real column in the bank; the thinly-covered ones — rare geometries, some coordinates — are flagged as places where a confident accuracy claim would rest on too few examples.) It is also where a new classifier feature earns its place: you add the feature, re-fit on the bank, and check whether it actually separates the types it was meant to.

The two libraries, side by side

detector fixture column bank
tests one value at a time a whole column
unit of data labeled values (+ generated negatives) labeled real columns
negatives generated by AutoType mutation naturally occurring (other columns)
ships in the package? yes (data_type_tests) no (development scaffolding)
develops new detectors new classifier features / routers

Together they mirror the two halves of the engine: the value library keeps the detectors precise, and the column library keeps the guesser honest about which types it can actually tell apart.
